description: Inventions written by hand for the sol-expert chatbot run on OpenStax Physics 2.2 and 2.3 (development material only): 20 sentences, 6 headings, 5 equations, 6 changed numbers, 6 changed words, 5 symbols added to real equations.
sentences: Objects with larger mass always reach a higher average speed than lighter objects over the same distance.
A good rule of thumb is that a healthy adult walks at about 1.4 meters per second on level ground.
Students often confuse speed and velocity, so it helps to say the direction out loud every time.
The fastest land animal, the cheetah, can sustain speeds near 29 meters per second for several minutes.
In practice, speedometers in cars measure the rotation rate of the wheels rather than the speed itself.
Remember that a negative velocity always means the object is slowing down.
This page was reviewed by an accessibility specialist before it was published here.
Tip: draw a quick sketch of the motion before you start any calculation, and label the origin.
Galileo first measured the acceleration of falling bodies by rolling bronze balls down inclined planes in 1604.
If you are using a screen reader, press H to jump between the headings of this page.
Air resistance has no effect on the motion described in these examples, so you can ignore friction entirely.
The equations in this section hold only when the acceleration is exactly zero for the whole trip.

Note that all of the quantities in this section must be converted to kilometers per hour before use.
